title: graph-types — the graph's types and laws

overview.l1: graph-types is the rulebook for the whole Bible Explorer project: it defines every kind of thing that can appear in the graph — verses, places, people, events, eras, kingdoms with borders, catechism paragraphs, commentary — and every kind of connection between them, like 'this verse cites that verse' or 'this event happened at this place.' It has ZERO external dependencies: everything here is plain, readable Rust. If this crate vanished, the server would lose its shared vocabulary for what a node or an edge even is, and the separate map project (a sibling codebase that depends on this crate too) would lose the exact same promise it's built on.
overview.l2: The crate is organized around a handful of ideas realized as Rust types. Identity (id.rs) uses generics and phantom types so a PlaceId and a PersonId are different types at compile time, even though both just wrap a string — mixing them up is a compile error. Text addressing (text.rs) generalizes 'verse reference' into a Corpus trait so the KJV and the (future) Book of Concord share one addressing scheme without either being Bible-shaped. Nodes (node.rs) are one big enum, NodePayload, with one variant per kind of thing; edges (edge.rs) are declared once through a relations! macro that generates matching forward/inverse labels so a connection can never disagree with its own reverse reading — the crate's single most load-bearing design decision. graph.rs assembles everything into one Graph struct and builds bidirectional indexes from it; explore.rs and store.rs define HOW you ask the graph questions (a trait-based query contract, GraphQuery, that any storage backend must satisfy identically to the in-memory Graph itself — proven by an executable conformance check, not just documentation). frontier.rs is the newest layer: an exhaustively-matched table deciding which popover sections show for which kind of thing. Every rule here either makes an illegal state impossible to construct, or names a law a test enforces.
overview.l3: Structurally: id.rs (identity/positions/content-addressing) and text.rs (corpus-generic addressing) have no crate-internal dependencies beyond each other and are imported by nearly everything else. node.rs (NodePayload/Node/Card) and chrono.rs (Year/TimePoint/DatePlacement/temporal_order) build on those. edge.rs is the crate's densest file (643 lines): the relations! macro (lines 42-70) generates RelationId/SymRelationId from one declarative list (lines 72-115), EdgeKind/dual (lines 118-130) make the forward/inverse bijection a shape rather than a tested property, and BiIndex::build/build_symmetric (lines 552-601) are the only functions that ever populate a relation's lookup tables. graph.rs's Graph struct (line 26) holds every row table plus the built indexes; build_indexes (line 120) is parallelized via std::thread::scope, with correctness verified against an independently-computed sequential reference (graph.rs:562). explore.rs's Holdings (line 149) realizes the spec's powerset-monad-over-positions design (§0's Explore newtype) — proven via literal left/right-identity and associativity tests in tests.rs — while PositionRef/Explorable is the paging-and-summary capability every position exposes. store.rs's GraphQuery trait (line 28) is the crate's port: Graph implements it as the canonical instance, MemStore/MemSnapshot is the reference in-memory backend, and assert_answers_match (line 242) is an executable law any future backend (a real database) must pass, proven to actually catch divergence via a deliberately lying snapshot test. frontier.rs is the most recently landed layer (dated 2026-09-07 in its own doc comments), compiling a per-(FocusKind, Capability) opt-in table as an exhaustive Rust match — the compiler itself refuses a missing cell. present.rs is declared but largely unwired scaffolding — no other file in the crate or the wider repo imports from it today. Two test surfaces close the loop: tests.rs (in-crate unit tests: monad laws, dual involution, bijection witness, temporal totality) and tests/toolchain_pin.rs (an integration test guarding the DefaultHasher-based id scheme against silent drift from a Rust compiler upgrade). Cargo.toml's empty [dependencies] table is the covenant made literal.

files.role: Build manifest: the zero-dependency covenant, made literal
files.l1: This is the smallest but most philosophically important file in the crate: its dependency list is empty, on purpose. The project's culture holds that the graph's core types shouldn't lean on anyone else's code — 'the compiler is the reviewer,' as the description field says. That's also why this crate compiles fast and why its rules (the ids, the node and edge shapes, the laws) are something any contributor can read end to end without first learning a pile of third-party libraries.
files.l2: A Cargo.toml is Rust's package manifest — the file cargo (Rust's build tool) reads to know a crate's name, version, edition, and dependencies. The [package] table (lines 1-5) names this crate atlas-graph-types; edition = 2021 pins which version of Rust's language rules apply (editions let the language evolve without breaking old code). The [dependencies] table (line 13) is EMPTY — no external crates are pulled in, which is unusual for a real-world Rust project and is exactly the point: everything the type system needs (hashing, collections, threads) comes from Rust's own standard library, which every Rust installation already includes.
files.l3: The comment block (lines 7-11) records a real workspace history event: this crate was once a standalone workspace (its own separate Cargo.lock) and was later folded into server/'s workspace as a member, unifying the lockfile across the whole project, once a parked concern (HOTFIX-7) that had motivated the earlier detachment was resolved. The comment also states the crate's tests still run in isolation via `cargo test -p atlas-graph-types` — the -p flag selects one package out of a workspace, exactly how this crate's law tests (tests.rs, tests/toolchain_pin.rs) are meant to be verified independently of the much larger server/ build. Zero dependencies is a genuine constraint, not an accident of a small crate: edge.rs's parallel index build uses std::thread::scope (standard library only) rather than reaching for rayon; id.rs's content hashing uses std::collections::hash_map::DefaultHasher rather than a real hashing crate (a documented, deliberate skeleton simplification per lib.rs's own module doc, guarded against compiler drift by graph-types/tests/toolchain_pin.rs). server/Cargo.toml and server/atlas-cli/Cargo.toml both declare atlas-graph-types as a path dependency, making this manifest's empty [dependencies] table load-bearing for the whole workspace's build graph, not just this one crate's.

files.role: Crate root: declares every module and the map-system's stable import surface
files.l1: This is the front door to the whole type system. It doesn't invent anything itself — it just lists every file in this crate as a module and republishes the handful of names other code should reach for (Graph, the id types, the text-locus types). It also carries a special 'covenant' list: an explicit, hand-maintained set of names that a sibling project (the separate map codebase) is allowed to depend on. If a name isn't on that list, the map project has no business importing it — that's the promise this file keeps.
files.l2: lib.rs is mostly `pub mod` declarations — Rust's way of saying 'this file is part of my crate, and its public items are reachable through it.' Each `pub mod id;` line pulls in id.rs etc. as a module, one of the two main things beside a crate (the whole compiled unit — this whole graph-types package) the vocabulary distinguishes. The `pub use` lines are re-exports: they let a caller write `atlas_graph_types::Graph` instead of `atlas_graph_types::graph::Graph`, flattening the module tree at the crate root. The `covenant` submodule is unusual: it's a second, narrower re-export list, documented as a promise rather than a convenience — anything imported through it is a stability commitment to another codebase (the map system), so growing it is a deliberate act, never a side effect of adding a pub item elsewhere. `#![allow(dead_code)]` at the top is an attribute telling the compiler not to warn about unused public items, appropriate for a types-first crate where many shapes exist before every consumer does. The final line, `#[cfg(test)] mod tests;`, compiles the tests module only when running `cargo test` — a feature-flag-like conditional compilation.
files.l3: lib.rs (73 lines) declares 11 modules (lines 16-26) and re-exports a curated surface at the crate root (lines 28-33): dual/Direction/EdgeId/EdgeKind/RelationId/SymRelationId from edge.rs, Explorable/Holdings from explore.rs, Graph from graph.rs, the store port types, AnyNodeId/NodeKind/Pid/Position/PositionKind from id.rs, and the locus types from text.rs. The `covenant` module (lines 40-70) is the load-bearing part: a second, EXPLICIT re-export list (never a wildcard — the doc comment calls this out: a wildcard would grow the promise silently) naming the exact chronology, justification, identity, and locus types the sibling map-system binds to (contract C1, dated 2026-08-24). Note the asymmetry versus the crate-root re-exports: `covenant` additionally exposes ContentAddressed, ContentHash, EventId/PlaceId/SourceId, Confidence/Provenance/ProvenanceId, and the full locus family, none of which the crate-root `pub use` block surfaces — two different audiences, two different promises. `#![allow(dead_code)]` (line 14) is a documented, deliberate suppression, not an oversight — see the module doc's 'skeleton notes' about Interned being a String stand-in and hashes being 64-bit DefaultHasher output rather than production multihashes. Every module here is exercised: `mod tests` at the bottom (`#[cfg(test)]`, line 73) wires in tests.rs, which the module doc comment calls 'the laws, run.'

files.role: Kind-tagged node identity, positions, and content-addressed pids
files.l1: Every place, person, event, and verse in the graph needs a name that can't be confused with a different kind of thing — a place id should never accidentally be used where a person id belongs. This file mints those names. It also defines the id for an edge-or-node position (so 'the thing you're looking at' can be either a node or a connection), and the content-addressing rule: an id derived from a hash of the thing itself, so a corrupted or tampered piece of data can never pretend to be something it isn't. Every verse card, place pin, and popover you click ultimately resolves through one of these ids.
files.l2: The star is `NodeId<K>` (line 67) — a generics-based, phantom-typed handle. `K: KindTag` is a trait-bound: K must implement KindTag, a tiny trait (line 36) whose only job is to carry a `const KIND: NodeKind`. The `kind_tags!` macro_rules (line 40) stamps out one zero-sized marker struct per node kind (PlaceTag, PersonTag, ...) so `NodeId<PlaceTag>` and `NodeId<PersonTag>` are DIFFERENT types even though both just wrap a String underneath — mixing them up is a compile error, not a runtime bug. The `PhantomData<K>` field is Rust's way of using a type parameter that carries no actual data at runtime; it exists purely to make the compiler track the tag. Because `#[derive(Clone, ...)]` would incorrectly require K itself to implement those traits, Clone/PartialEq/Ord/Hash are hand-written (lines 79-104) — a common Rust gotcha with phantom types. `AnyNodeId` (line 124) is the type-erased twin, used at API boundaries; `.narrow::<K>()` (line 131) is a checked downcast returning a Result, so a wrong-kind guess fails loudly instead of panicking. `ContentAddressed` (line 174) is a trait with a default method, `pid()`, built from `canonical_bytes()` via DefaultHasher.
files.l3: NodeKind (line 15) is the closed vocabulary (14 variants); KindTag (line 36) plus kind_tags! (line 40) generate one marker type + impl KindTag per kind, giving every one of the 14 `pub type XId = NodeId<XTag>` aliases (lines 106-119) real type-level distinctness backed by zero runtime cost (a NodeId is just a String + PhantomData). AnyNodeId::narrow (line 131) is the erased-to-typed boundary, proven fail-loud by tests.rs's kind_mismatch_is_a_checked_parse_not_a_surprise. Position (line 149) unifies Node(AnyNodeId) and Edge(EdgeId) — the 'edges are positions' law from the design spec (§3), letting a justification be walkable exactly like a node. ContentAddressed::pid() (line 177) hashes canonical_bytes() with std::collections::hash_map::DefaultHasher — the module doc in lib.rs flags this as a deliberate skeleton simplification (graph-types/tests/toolchain_pin.rs exists specifically because this hasher's output isn't guaranteed stable across Rust releases, so the toolchain itself is pinned). Tombstone (line 186) is declared but has no constructor or consumer in this crate yet — a disclosed gap, not a law. Every other file in the crate imports from here; it has one forward reference of its own, to crate::edge::EdgeId/EdgeKind inside Position/PositionKind (lines 151, 157), which is why id.rs and edge.rs are mutually referential modules within the one crate.

files.role: Text addressing: corpora, translation layers, and loci (a verse's exact address)
files.l1: This file answers the question 'where, exactly, in the text?' A verse reference like John 3:16 is one instance of the general idea here: a position inside some body of text (a corpus), optionally narrowed to a specific word range. The KJV is one corpus; the Book of Concord (Luther's catechism material) is set up to be another, using the exact same machinery. This is what lets a cross-reference, a quotation, or a catechism link point at a precise spot in the text, and what keeps Concord's own numbering from ever being mistaken for a Bible verse.
files.l2: Corpus (line 12) is a trait with an associated type, `type Ref: Ord + Clone + Debug` — each corpus (Bible, Concord) chooses its own reference type (VerseRef for the Bible, ConcordRef for Concord) while the rest of the crate writes code generic over `C: Corpus`. Locus<C> (line 104) is the generic address: a unit (C::Ref) plus an optional sub-span. Because `#[derive(...)]` on a generic struct would wrongly require C itself (not just C::Ref) to implement Clone/Eq/Ord/Hash, those impls are hand-written (lines 115-144) — the same pattern id.rs uses for NodeId<K>. BibleTag and ConcordTag (lines 37, 58) are zero-sized marker structs, the newtype pattern applied to generic dispatch rather than wrapping a value. TextRef (line 218) is the type-erased, corpus-tagged enum for the wire/UI boundary; narrowing back to a typed Locus is a checked Option-returning method (as_bible, line 242) rather than a panic. LocusSet<C> (line 202) wraps a BTreeSet — a sorted set — so a container's contents are always in deterministic order, which matters for the project's byte-identical build artifact. LayerMap (line 252) is a type-alias for BTreeMap<TranslationId, String>, one rendering per translation layer of one verse.
files.l3: Corpus::Ref: Ord (line 13) is the constraint that makes every downstream BTreeSet<Locus<C>>/BTreeMap possible — total ordering is required for determinism, not just convenience. TokenSpan::new (line 86) and LocusRange::new (line 157) both return Result, refusing an inverted span/range at construction (SpanError::Inverted) rather than trusting a caller — illegal states unrepresentable. BibleLocus/ConcordLocus/BibleLocusRange (lines 146-147, 197) are type aliases over the generic Locus<BibleTag>/Locus<ConcordTag>/LocusRange<BibleTag>, the concrete instantiations most of the rest of the crate actually names. TextLocus (line 224) is corpus-erased and is what most edge rows (edge.rs's Mentions, CrossRef, CatechismLink) actually store, since an edge like 'cites' can point across corpora; From<BibleLocus> for TextLocus / From<ConcordLocus> for TextLocus (lines 229, 234) make widening free (no Result), while narrowing (as_bible) is checked — the spec's widening-free/narrowing-checked rule realized exactly. CorpusRole (line 22) — NormaNormans/NormaNormata/Reference — isn't enforced BY this file (no code here reads it to gate anything); it's registry data the KJV-inerrancy and Confesses-direction laws lean on elsewhere (edge.rs's Confesses doc comment). No dedicated test file exercises text.rs directly; its invariants are exercised indirectly wherever BibleLocusRange::new/Locus::whole appear in graph-types/src/tests.rs and graph.rs's own test module.

files.role: What a node IS: identity + payload, for every kind of thing in the graph
files.l1: This is the master list of 'facts about a thing' — what a Place node actually carries (its name, coordinates, other names it's called), what an Event carries (its label, the verses that describe it, its witnesses), what a Person, an Era, a Polity (a kingdom with borders) carries, and so on for every kind of node. If you've ever seen a verse card, a place pin's tooltip, or a kingdom's border color on the map, that data came from a NodePayload defined here. card() at the bottom turns any node into the one-line label used to represent it before you click for more.
files.l2: NodePayload (line 62) is one big enum with one variant per node kind, each carrying its own named fields — Rust enums let each variant have a totally different shape, unlike many languages' enums. Matching on it (`match n.payload() { NodePayload::TextUnit { corpus, .. } => ... }`) is pattern-matching: the compiler checks every arm is handled, so adding a 15th node kind here forces every match site in the crate to acknowledge it (no silent gap). Several fields use Option<T> — 'maybe a value' — for facts that are only sometimes known: a Person's `birth_year: Option<i32>` is None for the overwhelming majority of biblical persons rather than a fake sentinel value. NodeData (line 181) is a small trait — the read-only interface every node satisfies — kept deliberately separate from Card/Presentable (present.rs), so 'what a node IS' and 'how it's displayed' never tangle. Node (line 173) implements both NodeData and ContentAddressed (id.rs's trait); its canonical_bytes() (line 200) formats the id and a debug string of the payload — the byte form its content-hash id derives from. card() (line 223) is a free function (not a method) that builds the one universal Card view via one big match, using Rust's `|` pattern-or syntax (line 228) to group several enum variants that share the same label field shape into one arm.
files.l3: NodePayload (line 62) has 14 variants; the doc comments are the crate's densest historical record of ruling reversals — e.g. Event's payload was WIDENED then re-NARROWED (lines 68-83: widened to a real payload, then narrowed to narrative-only) specifically so chronology can never live in two places (payload vs. dated-by edges) and disagree; that's a real invariant, not just prose — nothing in Event's fields duplicates from_year/to_year. EventWitnessPayload (line 25) and PolityEraPayload/PolityDeltaPayload (lines 39, 51) are plain data mirrors of richer types living in server/atlas-core (atlas_core::data::EventWitness/PolityDelta/PolityEra), deliberately kept FULLY STRUCTURED rather than flattened to display strings, and `translations` on EventWitnessPayload is a BTreeMap rather than the source's HashMap specifically for build-artifact byte-determinism (lines 19-23). Node::canonical_bytes (line 200) is a placeholder hash form (`format!(...)`), not the real Merkle-style canonical byte form the spec's §1 describes — a disclosed skeleton simplification consistent with lib.rs's own note. card() (line 223) is the one place that must stay exhaustive over NodePayload's variants; no dedicated test file targets node.rs, but graph.rs's own `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` and store.rs's `mod laws` both construct Node/NodePayload values directly and would break on a payload shape drift.

files.role: Day-capable time: dating, sequencing, and the one total temporal order
files.l1: This file is how the project knows 'which happened first' without ever putting a fake, invented date on anything. An event's date comes from one of a few honest sources — it's anchored to a known point in time, it's dated relative to a king's reign, it's simply 'after this other event,' or it's just placed within an era. Whatever the source, everything funnels into one function, temporal_order, that can always say which of two placements comes first — that's what lets the map's time slider and the reader's chronology sections agree with each other.
files.l2: Year (line 12) is a newtype wrapping i32, but its constructor Year::new (line 15) returns a Result and rejects 0 — there is no year zero in this calendar, and the invariant lives in the ONE place values get created rather than being re-checked by every caller. TimePoint (line 37) similarly validates in its constructor (day without month is an error) — both are examples of Rust's 'make illegal states unrepresentable' idiom: once you hold a Year or TimePoint, you know it's already valid. DatePlacement (line 83) is an enum naming the only four ways an event's timing can be justified; ChronoTarget (line 92) is the type-erased shape a dated-by edge actually points at (heterogeneous: an anchor, a prior event, or an era), derived from DatePlacement via the .target() method (line 99) using pattern-matching. temporal_order (line 144) returns std::cmp::Ordering and chains three comparisons with `.then_with(|| ...)` — a closure-based idiom for 'compare by this, then break ties by that.' `#[derive(PartialOrd, Ord)]` on TimePoint/ResolvedDate (lines 36, 60) gets field-by-field lexicographic ordering for free, in declaration order.
files.l3: DatedBy (line 122) is the authored row; PlacementBasis (line 113) — Textual vs Traditional — records whether a date comes straight from the text or from confessionally-acceptable traditional chronology, with the Justification on the SAME row carrying the why (edge.rs's Justification, imported at line 7) — a single carrier, never a second parallel reason field. SeqKey (line 133) breaks ties among events that share one TimePoint — the traditional-chronology ordering the project adopts for, e.g., a sequence of reign-year events all falling in the same year — and temporal_order (line 144) is explicitly documented TOTAL (no cluster of uncertainty ever reaches a surface), proven by tests.rs::temporal_order_is_total_and_antisymmetric, which checks reflexivity, antisymmetry, and totality over five hand-built ResolvedPlacements from David's reign. ChronoTarget (line 92) is graph.rs's build_indexes's dispatch target when lowering dated_by rows into the DatedBy relation's edge pairs (graph.rs:197-205) — every DatePlacement variant maps to exactly one ChronoTarget variant via .target(), so the edge-lowering code cannot miss a case. This whole module is part of the crate's covenant surface (lib.rs:43-46, there is no second dating path) — the map project imports ChronoTarget/DatePlacement/ResolvedPlacement/Year/etc. directly, so a signature change here is a promise-breaking act, not a routine refactor.

files.role: Edge kinds, the relation manifest, and the bidirectional index builder
files.l1: This is the file that says what KINDS of connections are allowed between things in the graph — cites, located-at, quotes, follows-in, and so on — and, crucially, guarantees that every connection reads the same from both ends: if verse A cites verse B, then verse B is automatically cited-by verse A, with no separate step and no chance for the two readings to disagree. It's also where the actual connection data lives (which verse cites which, which event happened where) before it gets indexed for fast lookup. Every 'X cross-references Y' or 'this event was located at that place' fact you see in the app is a row defined here.
files.l2: The relations! macro_rules invocation (lines 72-115) is the single declaration site: list a relation name plus its forward/inverse display labels once, and the macro (defined lines 42-70) expands it into a RelationId enum variant, a SymRelationId variant for symmetric relations, and the label lookup functions — one list, several generated pieces, so they can't drift apart. Direction (line 18) is a two-variant enum with .flip() (line 24); EdgeKind (line 120) wraps either Directed(RelationId, Direction) or Symmetric(SymRelationId), and dual() (line 125) flips a directed kind's direction while leaving a symmetric kind alone — a pattern-matching function that can't get the bijection wrong because there's nothing but a two-armed match to write. Each relation's actual data is a struct (e.g. Attests, line 232; LocatedAt, line 274) carrying `provenance: ProvenanceId` and `justification: Justification` on every authored row — the project's every-claim-carries-its-why rule made structural. BiIndex (line 552) is built, never hand-authored: BiIndex::build (line 558) takes a relation's rows as (subject, object, meta) tuples and produces both a forward and inverse BTreeMap in one pass — an iterator-driven loop, not two separate builder calls.
files.l3: relations! (macro, lines 42-70) is the crate's #[macro_export]ed, covenant-listed macro (lib.rs:69's own note) — a sibling crate can invoke it to declare its OWN relation manifest with the same drift-proof shape. 17 directed relations and 5 symmetric relations are declared (lines 73-114); Contains and Succession each have TWO row implementations lowering into one relation (documented at lines 78-86, 216-222 — Contains<C> vs plain content, Succession vs CanonSuccession) — one relation, two row shapes is a deliberate, reviewed pattern, not drift. EdgeId (line 146) is content-derived: entry_id (line 605) and entry_id_symmetric (line 625) both hash (relation, subject, object) via ContentAddressed, and the symmetric variant sorts the pair first (`if a <= b`) so hashing from either end produces the identical id — the literal bijection witness, proven by tests.rs::bijection_witness_same_edge_id_from_either_end and graph.rs's own ..._both_ways tests. Ground/GroundTarget (lines 159, 167) are near-duplicate enums (Scripture/Anchor/Source) that exist because Justification.grounds needs Ord/Hash for its BTreeSet, while JustifiedBy's edge target doesn't — a disclosed near-duplication, not an oversight. Relation (line 533) is a minimal trait (type Row, const ID, endpoints()) — thinner than the design spec's §3 sketch (which also carried typed Subject/Object associated types); this crate's realization erases endpoint types to Position earlier than the spec envisioned. BiIndex::build/build_symmetric (lines 558, 584) are the exact functions graph.rs's build_indexes calls per-relation, in parallel, via std::thread::scope — this file has no thread code itself, but its per-chunk purity (no shared mutable state) is what makes that safe.

files.role: Provenance vocabulary: who asserts a claim, and how confidently
files.l1: Every fact in this graph came from somewhere — a source document, an editorial decision, a derived computation — and this tiny file is where 'who says so, and how sure are we' lives. It's deliberately separate from 'why is this true,' which is a different concept (justification, defined in edge.rs) living elsewhere. If you've ever wondered why a verse card shows a little provenance note, this is the vocabulary behind it.
files.l2: Provenance (line 19) is a plain struct: a SourceId, a `locator: String` (where in that source), and a Confidence. Confidence (line 29) is a four-variant enum ranking how much standing a piece of text or data has — CanonicalText is reserved for Scripture specifically (per the corpus-role law in text.rs), so an adapter importing extrabiblical prose can never accidentally claim canonical status just by picking the wrong enum value elsewhere. ProvenanceId (line 14) is a type-alias for Interned (itself a String today) — a lightweight handle rather than the full Provenance struct, used on almost every edge row in edge.rs and graph.rs as the `provenance: ProvenanceId` field.
files.l3: The module doc comment (lines 1-10) is a rare piece of history-as-code: it records that the design spec's full ingestion machinery (a SourceAdapter trait, an Assertion IR, BoundaryLaw) was deliberately deleted from this crate under a dead-code law once the actual server pipeline (server/atlas-graph's per-source adapter modules) delivered the same contract concretely, with fidelity checks living inline in that crate instead. That's a disclosed, owner-ordered simplification, not drift — a future plugin-style source contract would be re-derived from the spec, not resurrected from git history. Confidence::CanonicalText (line 30) is the single enum value the CorpusRole law (text.rs:22) hangs off of: CanonicalText iff NormaNormans is stated as a comment here and in text.rs, not enforced by a compiled check in this crate — the enforcement lives in the server's adapters. No dedicated test file targets ingest.rs directly; ProvenanceId string literals appear throughout tests.rs and graph.rs's test module, but nothing here asserts the Confidence-to-CorpusRole law itself.

files.role: The Graph: per-relation tables, index-building, and the windowed reading query
files.l1: This is the actual graph, assembled: one big struct holding every table of nodes and every table of connections (attestations, cross-references, successions, and so on), plus the fast lookup indexes built from them. build_indexes is the one function that turns 'a pile of rows we've authored or imported' into 'a graph you can actually click through' — every popover frontier you've ever opened was served from an index this function built. reading_window is the simple, single primitive behind paging through a book of the Bible: give it a starting point and a count, and it hands back that slice of the corpus's reading order.
files.l2: Graph (line 26) is a plain struct of Vecs and BTreeMaps — 'the tables ARE the indexes' design principle means there's no generic Vec<Edge> with a stringly-typed kind; each relation gets its own typed field (`pub attests: Vec<Attests>`, etc.). build_indexes (line 120) is the single largest function in the crate: it walks every row table, converts each row into (Position, Position, EdgeMeta) pairs keyed by RelationId/SymRelationId in a BTreeMap, then calls BiIndex::build/build_symmetric (edge.rs) to produce both directions of lookup. The standard-library feature worth knowing here is std::thread::scope (line 405) — scoped-threads, a way to spawn threads guaranteed to finish before the scope block ends, so they can safely borrow &self data without Arc/Mutex; this is safe specifically because each chunk of rows is read-only and independent (no shared mutable state crosses a thread boundary). reading_window (line 496) is a small method using iterator adapters (`.skip(start).take(n)`) over a Vec<AnyNodeId>. The nested `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` (line 515) is itself worth noting: tests can live in the same file as the code they test, gated to compile only under cargo test.
files.l3: build_indexes (lines 120-492) has a documented performance history (PERF-2b, lines 100-119): it was parallelized with std::thread::scope, measured roughly 2.6x faster for index-building alone and roughly 1.9x for the whole artifact-load path on a 16-core machine (see server/BENCHMARKS.md), with chunk sizes derived from std::thread::available_parallelism() rather than a flat constant (a flat 50k-row chunk size under-parallelized pid_index specifically, per the inline note at lines 370-386). Correctness under parallelism is proven, not assumed: parallel_build_indexes_matches_sequential_over_a_large_relation (line 562) drives 300 real Attests rows through the real build_indexes() and compares the result key-for-key, IN ORDER, against an independently computed sequential BiIndex::build — guarding specifically against a merge-order bug that would only show up with a position spanning more than one chunk. text_node (line 86) is the one hand-written mapping from a TextLocus to its skeleton-position AnyNodeId (bible/{book}.{chapter}.{verse} or concord/{part}.{article}.{paragraph}) — every text-anchored relation (Attests, CommentsOn, Cites, Quotes, Confesses, Fulfillment, Typology) routes through it when lowering to edge pairs. ContainerContent::Container rows (lines 141, 166) are the genuinely-recursive containment case — book contains chapter — proven both-ways by container_child_and_canon_succession_rows_lower_into_the_existing_indexes_both_ways (line 669). The struct's own doc comments are an unusually explicit changelog of what got wired up when (contains_concord, comments_on, spoken_by/spoken_at, analogue were all declared fields for a time before their lowering loops existed) — a real, disclosed pattern of field-declared-wiring-deferred-then-closed worth knowing before assuming every pub field here is live in build_indexes.

files.role: Exploration: the Explorable capability and the Holdings powerset monad
files.l1: This is the file that makes 'clicking around the graph' actually work. PositionRef answers two questions for any node or edge: 'how many connections of each kind do you have' (for deciding which sections of a popover to even show) and 'give me one page of a specific kind of connection' (for actually listing them, with paging so a hub node with thousands of connections doesn't dump them all at once). Holdings is the slightly more advanced idea behind multi-hop questions like 'what happened at the same place as this event' — it's a set of everywhere you're currently standing, and taking a step follows one kind of connection from everywhere in that set at once, pooling the results.
files.l2: Explorable (line 50) is a trait with two methods, edge_summary and edges — deliberately NOT including anything about display, which lives elsewhere (present.rs). PositionRef (line 57) is a newtype-style wrapper around Position that implements it. raw_neighbors (line 59) is a private helper doing the actual pattern-matching over EdgeKind: for a Directed kind it looks up the right BTreeMap (fwd or inv) inside the relation's BiIndex; for Symmetric it always reads fwd (since a symmetric relation has no inverse direction to hold). EdgeQuery/EdgePage (lines 12, 40) implement cursor-based paging: `cursor: Option<usize>` is 'maybe a starting offset' — None means start from the beginning — and EdgePage.next is Some(offset) if there's more, None if you've reached the end, the classic Rust way of representing an optional continuation without a sentinel value. Holdings (line 149) wraps a BTreeSet<Position> — a sorted, deduplicated collection; .bind() (line 160) takes a closure (`impl Fn(&Position) -> Holdings`) and unions the results across every held position — this is literally a monadic bind, and the crate's tests (tests.rs) check it obeys the three monad laws.
files.l3: Explorable/PositionRef (lines 50, 57) are the trait/impl pair that store.rs's `GraphQuery for Graph` delegates straight to (store.rs:60-65) — this file is the ONLY place raw_neighbors exists, so both the summary and paging paths, and GraphQuery's public methods, share one source of truth for what counts as a neighbor. Holdings::step (line 170) is the Kleisli arrow the design spec's §0 Haskell sketch names `step :: EdgeKind -> NodeId -> Exploration NodeId`; .steps() (line 182) folds a slice of EdgeKinds to compose multiple hops. inverse_entry_ids (line 189) is the crate's executable bijection witness: it takes every forward neighbor of a position, asks the DUAL kind for its own back-reference, and returns the (forward_edge_id, inverse_edge_id) pairs — tests.rs::bijection_witness_same_edge_id_from_either_end asserts every pair is equal. EdgeMeta (line 26) is documented as an intentionally CLOSED, deliberately-extended enum (line 24: extending this enum is a deliberate act reviewed like any relation change) — it exists because earlier client code once worked around the lack of per-entry annotation (which narrative a succession edge belongs to; a citation's vote rank) with an ad hoc client-side lookup; this closes that gap at the type level. Holdings implements the powerset monad from the design spec's §0 conceptual spine, realized here without the payload half — this crate's Holdings is the pure-position special case; left/right identity and associativity are proven in tests.rs's monad_* tests, and step_page_agreement_pages_are_windows_over_the_total (tests.rs:135) proves paged access through PositionRef::edges agrees exactly with the unpaged Holdings::step.

files.role: The storage port: GraphQuery contract, MemStore, and the conformance law
files.l1: This is the promise the rest of the app makes about how it will ask questions of the graph — 'give me this node,' 'how many connections of each kind leave here,' 'one page of those connections,' 'the next twenty verses.' Any storage that can keep that promise can sit underneath the app, which is what lets the project swap its storage later (say, to a real database) without touching the reader or the map. MemStore is the simplest thing that keeps the promise today — an in-memory, versioned holder of compiled graphs. assert_answers_match is the referee: it can compare any two things that keep the promise and fail loudly the instant they disagree.
files.l2: GraphQuery is a trait — Rust's version of an interface: a list of method signatures (node, derive, edge_summary, edges, reading_window) that a type promises to implement. Graph itself implements it (line 50) — the 'canonical instance' law: the real graph answers its own contract, so there's no separate reference implementation to keep in sync. `GraphSnapshot: GraphQuery` (line 74) is a trait with a trait-bound supertrait — anything that's a snapshot must ALSO be a full GraphQuery, plus carry a version(). GraphVersion (line 23) wraps a ContentHash — a newtype. MemStore (line 161) holds versions in a `BTreeMap<GraphVersion, Arc<Graph>>`; Arc (atomic reference count) is what lets multiple open snapshots share one immutable Graph cheaply, without cloning the whole graph per reader. assert_answers_match (line 242) is a free function, not a trait method — it takes `candidate: &impl GraphQuery` (a generic parameter constrained by a trait, resolved at compile time) and a `model: &Graph`, and walks every known position asking both the same questions, using Rust's assert_eq!/assert! panic macros to fail with a precise message at the first divergence.
files.l3: GraphQuery (line 28) is deliberately thin — five methods — and MemSnapshot's impl (line 134) is PURE DELEGATION to the wrapped Graph, so conformance is visible in the code, not just tested. position_inventory (line 195) is the subtle part of the conformance harness: it doesn't just walk model.nodes (which could be sparse), it also unions in every Position appearing as a KEY in any built index — the doc comment (lines 191-194) says this exists specifically so a sparse node table cannot produce a vacuously-passing check, and conformance_harness_catches_a_lying_snapshot (line 397) proves it: a deliberately lying GraphQuery impl that drops one edge entry per page is caught even when the underlying node table only has ONE real node. assert_answers_match (line 242) checks node/derive/edge_summary for every position, then edges at TWO limits per inhabited kind ([1, count.max(1)], line 264) specifically to exercise both single-item paging and one-shot full pages. version_of (line 102) is a stand-in Merkle root: hashes every node's id+payload debug string, sorted by BTreeMap iteration order — real determinism today, but a placeholder for the spec's true Merkle structure over every referenced pid. The `mod laws` tests (line 292) cover: atomic publish + snapshot immutability (line 344), content-addressed dedup (line 365), self-verifying derive (line 373), the conformance law against both a matching and a lying snapshot, and reading-window partition-invariance through the port (line 438). GraphPublisher/GraphStore (lines 91, 79) exist as ports for a future non-memory backend (a real database) to implement against this exact same test suite.

files.role: The frontier contract: which sections show on which focus kind, compiled as an exhaustive table
files.l1: When you click a verse, a place, or an event, the popover that opens shows some sections and not others — cross-references here, but not there; a chronology strip on an event, but not on a place. This file is the single, compiled rulebook for exactly that: for every kind of thing you can focus on, and every kind of section that COULD show, it says yes or no. Nothing about that decision lives in scattered client code anymore — it's one table, and because it's written as Rust's exhaustive match, the compiler itself refuses to let anyone add a new focus kind or a new section type without deciding every new cell explicitly.
files.l2: FocusKind (line 101) is a plain enum of every clickable kind (Verse, Place, Event, ...) — deliberately NOT the same as id.rs's NodeKind, because the app has focus kinds (like Chapter, Year) that don't correspond to a real graph node yet. FocusBacking (line 123) is the type-checked bridge between the two vocabularies: Node(NodeKind) (a real node exists today), NodeDesignate(NodeKind) (will exist, doesn't yet), or ParameterizedView (never a node — it's a computed query). Capability (line 209) is the enum of section families (CrossReferences, Chronology, ...), and .edges() (line 356) is a const fn — a function evaluable at compile time — returning the exact EdgeKinds (relation + direction) that capability walks, so a consumer can feed the result straight into Holdings::step from explore.rs. allows() (line 496) is the payoff: a single `match (kind, cap)` over BOTH enums at once — Rust checks this is EXHAUSTIVE, meaning every (kind, capability) pair must appear in some arm or the crate won't compile, exactly the guarantee the doc comments call out as the whole point.
files.l3: The smart-frontier rule (module doc, lines 29-45) states the law as a biconditional: a section displays iff instances exist for the focus AND the focus kind hasn't opted out of that capability. allows() (line 496) compiles the second half; the first half (whether real rows exist) is SectionOutcome (line 484), a documented but not-yet-wired three-valued type reserved for a future server response. FrontierEdge (line 199) pairs an EdgeKind with an `Option<NodeKind>` target — None is used honestly where a relation's target really is heterogeneous (TimeAndPlace's DatedBy edge, whose target is ChronoTarget, not one node kind) rather than guessed. Capability::ALL (line 332) and capability_edges_are_never_empty (line 596) together guarantee no capability can exist without at least one real edge behind it — tested exhaustively via iteration. The doc comments preserve an unusually complete paper trail of a design review (FQ-0, dated 2026-09-07): one fix replaced decorative cells naming relations with zero real rows (the original Parallels cell named a dead symmetric relation with zero producers); another fixed 'fictional' graph_kind() cells via FocusBacking; another carved three sections (place events, person mentions, catechism scriptures) out of a catch-all into their own governed cells. Only ONE consumer outside this crate was found by search: server/atlas-graph/tests/frontier_falsifiability.rs, which asserts a capability's named relation actually has rows in the compiled artifact — this crate cannot run that check itself (it has no compiled artifact to inspect), so the split is deliberate: shape here, falsifiability there. allows()'s own match arms (lines 502-584) are also the crate's most heavily-tested single function — ten tests in `mod tests` (line 588) pin specific rows (Verse's seven capabilities, Event's calibration row with no cross-references, the three escapee capabilities, Chapter/Book's Members+Chronology) individually, so a one-line cell edit that regresses a different kind is caught immediately.

files.role: Presentation policy scaffolding: surfaces, contexts, and the Presentable trait
files.l1: This file is the not-yet-finished twin of frontier.rs's rulebook: where that file says WHICH sections show, this one is meant to say HOW they render — as running text, as a map pin, as a timeline row. Right now it's mostly a set of named possibilities (Surface::Map, PresentationContext::Pin, ...) with one working example: turning a node's Card into a labeled bit of text or a map pin label. Nothing else in the crate calls into this file yet — it's a placeholder for real, data-driven display policy the project intends to grow here rather than hardcode into the client.
files.l2: Presentable (line 88) is a trait with one method, `present(&self, ctx, g) -> Presentation` — 'form policy: one implementation per (kind, context)' per the module doc, meaning the SAME Card renders differently depending on the PresentationContext it's asked for (line 19: Card, Entry, Inline, Heading, Pin, CitationRow, Marker). The one real `impl Presentable for Card` (line 92) uses a match over ctx, with `_ =>` as a catch-all pattern-matching arm for the contexts that don't yet have bespoke handling. focusable() and display() (lines 69, 74) are functions whose bodies are literally `true` and `FrontierPresentation::default()` — their doc comments say outright that the policy table lands with the app and the signature is the design, meaning these exist to PIN the function signature future code will fill in, not to do real work today.
files.l3: Surface (line 11), PresentationContext (line 19), Renderer (line 30), SectionStyle (line 38), and SectionOrder (line 45) are all enums with no logic consuming most of their variants yet — SectionSpec/FrontierPresentation (lines 53, 63) sketch a per-section render spec (a renderer, a style, a display `initial` clamp with the invariant that a hidden remainder must be signaled with the true count, stated in a comment but not yet enforced by any type or test). focusable/display (lines 69, 74) take `_surface`/`_kind` — the leading underscore is Rust's convention for an intentionally unused parameter, silencing the unused-variable warning while documenting that the eventual real implementation WILL use them. This file is imported by nothing else in the crate (no other graph-types module has `use crate::present`), and a repo-wide search found no consumer outside the crate either — it's dormant scaffolding, honestly incomplete rather than silently broken. No dedicated tests exist for it; the one `impl Presentable for Card` block is exercised by nothing beyond what a future caller would add. Treat this file as a stated INTENTION (per-kind, per-context render policy travels as data — a stylesheet can never re-decide a law) rather than working machinery today.

files.role: The crate's own law tests: monad laws, dual involution, bijection, temporal totality
files.l1: This file is where the project proves its own rules actually hold, using a small made-up 'toy graph' (three fake biblical events with locations and an order). It checks things like: does following a connection and then following it backwards get you back where you started? Does composing two multi-step questions give the same answer regardless of how you group the steps? Is 'which of these two dates comes first' always answerable, with no ties left dangling? If this file's tests are green, the crate's central design claims are demonstrated, not just asserted.
files.l2: This is a unit-test module, compiled only under `#[cfg(test)]` (wired in from lib.rs:73). toy() (line 33) builds a small Graph by hand — three chained events (Succession), two Attests rows, two LocatedAt rows — then calls `g.build_indexes()`, exactly like real code would. The monad_* tests (lines 109-132) check the three laws any proper monad must satisfy — left identity, right identity, associativity — using Holdings::focus/.bind/.step from explore.rs; each test is a direct, literal translation of the mathematical law into an assert_eq!. step_page_agreement_pages_are_windows_over_the_total (line 135) drains a paginated query one item at a time (limit: 1) in a loop, collecting into a BTreeSet, and checks the total matches the un-paged Holdings::step result — proving paging is honest, not just fast. temporal_order_is_total_and_antisymmetric (line 218) builds five ResolvedPlacements and checks every pair compares consistently, including that swapping the arguments always reverses the Ordering (.reverse()).
files.l3: Ten tests total (lines 82-264). dual_is_involutive_over_every_kind (line 82) iterates RelationId::ALL times both Directions plus SymRelationId::ALL, checking `dual(dual(k)) == k` for directed kinds and `dual(k) == k` (a fixed point) for symmetric ones — a genuinely exhaustive check over the manifest, not a spot check. bijection_witness_same_edge_id_from_either_end (line 155) calls explore::inverse_entry_ids and asserts every (fwd, inv) pair is literally equal — the crate's most direct proof of the one-row-two-projections-one-id law. edge_summary_includes_symmetric_kinds (line 181) and edge_summary_counts_match_frontiers (line 206) both guard the honesty policy (a summary lists ONLY kinds with count greater than 0, and the count it reports must exactly match what walking that kind actually returns) — the former specifically regression-guards a fixed bug (a review comment notes symmetric kinds were once silently excluded from summaries). kind_mismatch_is_a_checked_parse_not_a_surprise (line 247) and malformed_chains_fail_to_construct (line 254) are the crate's fail-loud-constructor checks, covering AnyNodeId::narrow (id.rs) and Succession::new (edge.rs) respectively. Every test here constructs its own toy graph rather than depending on any compiled artifact — this crate has no I/O and no file dependencies at test time (aside from graph-types/tests/toolchain_pin.rs, a separate integration test file with a different purpose).

files.tests: this file IS the test suite for id.rs, edge.rs, explore.rs, and chrono.rs's law-level behavior; it has no tests of its own beyond itself.

files.role: Integration test: the Rust compiler version itself is a pinned, checked law
files.l1: Every id in this project is, today, a hash produced by a specific piece of the Rust standard library — one that Rust's own documentation warns may change between releases. If the compiler version drifted, every single id in the compiled graph could silently change even though nothing about the actual Bible data changed. This file exists purely to make that impossible to overlook: it checks that a file naming the exact allowed compiler version exists, and that the compiler which built this very test binary IS that exact version — if someone runs a compiler update, these tests fail loudly instead of letting ids drift quietly.
files.l2: This is an integration test file — it lives in graph-types/tests/ rather than inside src/, which in Rust means it's compiled as its own separate test binary that exercises the crate from the outside, the same way an external consumer would. repo_root() (line 15) uses the env! macro to read CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR (a compile-time environment variable Cargo sets) and builds a PathBuf (a heap-allocated, owned filesystem path) pointing one directory up, to the repo root. channel_from (line 20) parses rust-toolchain.toml by hand with iterator methods (.lines(), .find_map()) rather than pulling in a TOML-parsing dependency — consistent with the crate's zero-dependency covenant. The tests use std::process::Command (Command-process) to actually RUN `rustc --version` and check its output starts with the pinned string — this is genuinely executing an external program from within a test, not just reading a file.
files.l3: PINNED = 1.97.1 (line 13) is checked three independent ways: rust_toolchain_toml_pins_the_exact_version (line 29) parses rust-toolchain.toml at the repo root and asserts its channel field equals the pin exactly (never a moving name like stable); the_compiler_that_built_this_test_is_the_pinned_version (line 41) derives the rustc binary path from the CARGO env var Cargo sets at build time (`.with_file_name` on Windows) — this checks the ACTUAL compiler that built this test binary, not just whatever rustc happens to be first on PATH; rustup_resolves_the_pin_from_the_repo_root (line 57) instead runs the ~/.cargo/bin rustup proxy with current_dir set to the repo root, checking that rustup's own directory-based toolchain resolution independently lands on the same pin — a genuinely different failure mode from the second test (a stale proxy shim vs. a wrong build-time compiler). channel_parser_reads_the_toml_shape_we_write (line 78) is a small, fast sanity check on the hand-rolled TOML parser itself, covering both quoted and unquoted-equals spacing. The module doc comment (lines 1-8) explicitly ties this file's existence to id.rs's ContentAddressed::pid() using DefaultHasher — this is the law that makes that skeleton simplification safe to ship: the hash algorithm can't move because the compiler that defines it can't move. No production code in graph-types/src/ reads this file's pin at runtime; it is purely a CI/dev-machine guard.
